hook: They were told to lick the glowing paint. It was poison.
narration: They were told to lick the glowing paint. It was poison. In the 1910s, young women in American factories painted watch dials with a miracle substance called radium. It made the numbers glow in the dark, and soldiers and shoppers loved it. The women were paid well for steady, careful work. Their bosses told them to point the brushes with their lips, to keep the tips sharp. They were told it was harmless. Some of the women even painted their nails and teeth for fun, and laughed when they glowed in the dark. Then their teeth began to fall out. Their jaws crumbled. Their bones broke from the inside. Doctors had no answer, and the companies blamed disease, and even blamed the women themselves. But a few of them refused to stay quiet. They took the companies to court, one painful step at a time, some of them too weak to raise a hand to swear the oath. They won. And their fight led to the first real safety rules for workers handling radioactive material. Today, workers are protected because those women spoke up. So when someone tells you something is safe, ask who benefits from your silence, and who pays if they are wrong.
